Exploring the Devil’s Den in Elk County

By
Rusty Glessner
-
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:39
Instaread

Located deep within State Game Lands 44 in Elk County, the Devil’s Den is a massive sandstone rock formation stretching approximately 400 yards across a forested mountainside.

Featuring towering cliffs, enormous overhangs, narrow passages, and scenic overlooks, this geological attraction is one of the most impressive rock formations I’ve encountered during my travels across Pennsylvania.

I recently spent a November morning exploring and photographing Devil’s Den, and here’s my firsthand account of what makes this remote destination worth the hike.

Directions to Devil’s Den

The hike to Devil’s Den described here is 3.3 miles one-way (6.6 miles round-trip), beginning near Route 219 and following a series of gated forest roads through State Game Lands 44.

Much of the route follows an old railroad grade that has been repurposed as a buried natural gas pipeline right-of-way, making the walk essentially flat and relatively easy to navigate despite its length.

Along the way, you’ll encounter remnants of the area’s natural gas infrastructure, including pipeline markers, old wellheads, and access roads winding through the hardwood forest.

One of the highlights of this route is that it passes right by Umbrella Rock, one of Pennsylvania’s most unusual geological formations, making it possible to visit two fascinating natural landmarks on the same hike.

Several intersections require careful navigation, however, and because there are no trail signs or blazes, I strongly recommend screenshotting the map below or better yet, using a GPS-enabled hiking app such as onX, AllTrails, or FarOut.

To make your hike easier, I’ve included GPS coordinates for all the important turns, intersections, and points of interest along the route, including Umbrella Rock, Rocky Overlook, and both ends of Devil’s Den.

Since the entire hike takes place on State Game Lands 44, wearing a blaze orange cap and jacket or vest is strongly recommended year-round and required during applicable hunting seasons, including October 1 through January 31 and April 20 through May 31.

Exploring the Devil’s Den

Upon reaching Devil’s Den, the relatively ordinary forest landscape suddenly gives way to an extraordinary collection of towering sandstone cliffs and enormous boulders that seem to rise out of nowhere.

The formation is essentially divided into two massive rock complexes, a northern section and a southern section, connected by an elevated rocky ledge that provides access to several scenic viewpoints.

Exploring the southern section reveals enormous sandstone overhangs, sheltered alcoves, and narrow passages where massive rock walls rise high overhead.

Some of these natural corridors are large enough to walk through comfortably, while others squeeze between gigantic boulders whose surfaces display fascinating layers, textures, and erosion patterns.

The northern section is equally impressive, featuring sheer sandstone walls, dramatic projecting ledges, and unusually shaped rock formations that almost seem to defy gravity.

Throughout Devil’s Den, the sandstone exhibits remarkable examples of natural weathering, including honeycomb-like cavities, rounded depressions, and unusual shapes that resemble faces and animals.

Moss-covered boulders, ferns, and rhododendrons add another dimension to the scenery, particularly in the shaded crevices and sheltered spaces between the rocks.

The rocky ledge connecting the northern and southern formations offers fantastic 180-degree views to the north, south, and west, overlooking miles of forested hills and valleys.

I’ve included plenty of photographs featuring myself standing beside, beneath, and even atop these formations, because it’s nearly impossible to appreciate their enormous size without a person in the frame for scale.

Final Thoughts

Having explored and photographed countless rock formations across Pennsylvania, I can confidently say that Devil’s Den ranks among my personal favorites, thanks to its incredible size, variety of geological features, and opportunities for exploration and photography.

For anyone willing to tackle the 6.6-mile round-trip hike, Devil’s Den offers a rewarding opportunity to experience one of the most fascinating natural attractions in Elk County while enjoying the solitude and rugged beauty of State Game Lands 44.
